title: What can friendship survive?
claim: The book says those devoted to friendship do not leave a friend once made (791, நட்டபின் வீடில்லை) and that the world loves those who do not give up old friends (809), yet it calls leaving a fool's friendship gain (797) and orders the unfit dropped even at a price (800, ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக). It also says the bond grows with practice (783) yet does not need it (785), and on Manakkudavar's reading 785's quick bond sits against 792's demand to examine again and again. The growth question is settled by character, not time: the bond with பண்புடையார் deepens with practice (783), while with பண்பிலார் shrinking is better than growing (811), the waning that 782 observes in fools' friendship. Parimelazhagar supplies the limit on leaving: exit is for a friendship taken up without knowing (800).
limits: On Parimelazhagar's reading 785 only says feeling, more than contact, makes the bond, and there is no conflict with 783 or 792. Old friends who harm you are kept (807), which he treats as a separate case.

title: The friend is judged at the hour of ruin
claim: In all three books one moment decides a friendship: what the friend does when the other falls. The Book of Virtue says never abandon those who were a support in sorrow (106) and that their help is remembered through seven births (107); chapter 79 defines friendship as sharing the suffering in ruin (787) and acting there and then like a hand catching a slipping garment (788). The same measure condemns: the deserter's bond burns the heart even at death (799), those who fail at the crisis are an untrained horse worse than solitude (814, 798's ஆற்றறுப்பார்), and friends who give no safety are better never acquired (815). In the Book of Love, 1293 turns the saying that the ruined have no friends against the speaker's own heart, a deserter she cannot decline.
limits: This is one standard among several: other verses make rebuke (784, 795) or inner feeling (785, 786) the mark of friendship. 1293 is a lover's dramatised reproach quoting a saying, not a teaching about friends.

title: Learning that conduct cancels
claim: 391 asks for two things in order: learn without flaw, then stand in keeping with it. Several verses across the Books of Virtue and Wealth enforce the second half by withdrawing the status of the learned from those who skip it: whoever has learned much but cannot move in accord with the world is unlearned and without understanding (140); whoever has read, understood and taught but is not restrained is the greatest fool (834); wide understanding is worth nothing if one covets (175); and restraint after learning is what virtue itself seeks out (130). In statecraft and medicine the same rule becomes professional: knowing the method from the treatises, act knowing the world (637), and the learned physician must weigh this patient, this illness, this time (949).
limits: The verses do not claim that study produces good conduct; 823 says study rarely makes the unworthy good at heart, which is why 391 has to command conduct separately. The thread does not cover the question of where understanding comes from, treated in thread:knowing_and_learning.

title: Learning that is not spoken
claim: The book ranks learned people by whether they can deliver their learning before an audience, and is harsh to those who cannot. Those who cannot unfold what they learned are scentless flowers (650); those who cannot speak tellingly in a good assembly are useless however much they learned (728); and those who learned yet fear the assembly are lower than the unlearned (729), using the very word கடை that 395 gives the unlearned. Silence is therefore graded by who keeps it: it is the unlearned person's merit before the learned (403) and the learned person's disgrace. The positive title follows the same measure: 'learned among the learned' is whoever makes learning go home before the learned (722), and the envoy is judged the same way among treatise-holders and in a hostile court (683, 686, 724).
limits: These verses concern speech before assemblies and courts, mostly in the Book of Wealth's chapters on speech and assemblies; they do not say learning has no private worth (398 makes it a protection across births). 720 adds that an unfit audience wastes even good speech.
